editorial.headline: Wholesale Footwear: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This wholesale footwear activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but a foreign investor cannot register it as PMA in Bali under the island-wide risk moratorium.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, the decisive fact comes first: this activity cannot be registered as a PMA business in Bali at present. That does not alter its national standing; it clarifies the practical divide between a nationally open activity and Bali’s separate, island-wide restriction on PMA registrations in Low and Medium-Low risk classes. For a founder considering Bali as the operating base, that distinction is not a footnote—it is the starting point.

The activity itself is wholesale trade in footwear: shoes, sandals and slippers. It sits in the commercial layer that moves finished footwear through the market in volume, rather than defining the making of the product or its sale in a retail setting. The scope is therefore direct and recognisable: businesses dealing in footwear at wholesale, with the category expressly encompassing those principal forms of footwear.

Registration is open across the full range of listed business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. At national level, this activity carries TERBUKA PMA status and permits foreign ownership up to 100%. In plain terms, the national framework permits full foreign ownership for this activity. The cited national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That position matters because it confirms that the foreign-investment question is not closed at the national level; the constraint arises from the Bali-specific treatment of the activity.

In Bali, the record classifies the activity as Blocked (risk class). At the Besar scale, its OSS risk classification is Low or Medium-Low across every stated scope, bringing it within Bali’s permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. The stated reason records that block as applying under the Bali moratorium in May 2026. The result is unequivocal: national openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling do not create a route for PMA registration in Bali for this activity. A founder may read the national position as permissive, but must treat the Bali restriction as controlling for a Bali-based PMA registration.
